newsitem.title: FRANCE: FOCUS-FRENCH INSURER GAN IN PROPERTY SALE.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-FRENCH INSURER GAN IN PROPERTY SALE.

text.p: Clearing the decks for its privatisation, state-controlled insurer GAN announced on Friday a deal to sell a portfolio of distressed real estate carrying a gross value of three billion francs ($476.6 million).

The insurer, struggling to dig its way out of a long-running real estate slump, identified the buyers as U.S. investment bank Morgan Stanley and Constructa, a property firm headquartered in Paris and Miami with activities in Europe and the United States.

A spokeswoman for GAN, whose property woes at one time threatened to engulf the company, would not disclose the sale price. But GAN said in a statement it was more than estimates used last December to set the cost of state support required for the insurer.
The European Union last week cleared government plans to pump 20 billion francs into GAN, stipulating in return that the insurer must be privatised by June 30 next year at the latest.
Market sources earlier had said they believed the assets were worth up to one billion francs.

GAN said in May its aim was to sell 3.8 billion francs of net assets with a gross value of 16.9 billion francs in the following months as part of its restructuring ahead of privatisation. The property was acquired at the peak of the market before prices went into a tailspin in the early 1990s.
In June, GAN sold a Paris office property.

Some 75 properties were covered by the auction handled by U.S. bank Bankers Trust. Commercial properties made up 54 percent, offices composed 38 percent while the rest was housing. More than 60 percent was in the Paris region.

Loss-making GAN is the latest in a run of French financial institutions to seek to unload property whose value has dived as much as 70 percent. So far, the big buyers have been U.S. "vulture funds" which have earned huge sums snapping up unwanted U.S. real estate and hope to replicate their success in Europe.
Property specialists said what set the GAN sale apart was that it was one of the first major sales of physical assets rather than property loans which take a long time to recover.
Others firms which sources said had been interested included Whitehall Street Real Estate LP, General Electric Capital Corp, Lehman Brothers and Wilshire Financial Services Group.
The property assets had been put in Baticredit and Parixel, two special companies designed to hold distressed property that were set up when GAN's real estate troubles reached a pitch.
Insurer AGF announced on Monday it sold 16 Paris properties for 850 million francs to French mutural insurer MAAF, generating a 22 million franc capital gain.
French property specialists forecast transaction volumes will rise to around 15 billion francs this year from just over 10 billion last year but expect prices to remain weak.
